name: AI for Program Delivery and Impact
objectives: Given a list of program results, identify which are outputs and which are outcomes, getting at least 4 of 5 right
Given a public description of one program, build a one-page logic model with inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes with AI's help, with everything you do not really do removed
Given an outcome, choose two simple measures your team can collect, asked before and after, that are honest and realistic for your staff and volunteer time
Given your outcome measures, write a short, anonymous participant survey of 5 to 8 questions with AI, with no leading questions and a note that it is voluntary
Given anonymous survey counts, summarize the results with AI and check every percent yourself, with no detail that could identify a person
Given your logic model and checked results, write a one-page impact report with the need, what you did, what changed, a story and a lesson learned, with no numbers or claims that are not in your data

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Outputs and outcomes: what is the difference?
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Tell outputs and outcomes apart for one of your programs.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of program results, you will identify which are outputs and which are outcomes, getting at least 4 of 5 right.
Outputs count what you did: 300 meals served, 40 tutoring sessions, 25 volunteers trained. Outcomes describe what changed for people: families worried less about food, students raised their reading grades, volunteers felt ready to lead.
Funders and boards increasingly ask for outcomes, not just outputs. Outcomes show your mission is working.
AI can help you think it through. Ask: "Our program [public description] does [activities]. List likely outputs and likely short-term outcomes for participants." Then choose the ones that are true for your program.
Words to know:
- Output: a count of what your program did, like meals served.
- Outcome: a change in people's lives because of your program.
- Impact: the bigger, longer-term difference your work makes in the community.
Try it now: For one program, write three outputs and two outcomes. Use AI to brainstorm, then keep only the ones true for your program.
You can now tell outputs from outcomes for your own program.

check.q: "25 volunteers trained" is an example of what?
check.why: Outputs count what you did; outcomes describe what changed for people.

check.q: Your report lists only meals served. A funder asks for outcomes. What do you add?
options: What changed for families, such as worrying less about food
check.why: Outcomes describe what changed for people because of the program.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building a simple logic model
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a one-page logic model for one program with AI's help.
This lesson builds toward: Given a public description of one program, you will build a one-page logic model with inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes with AI's help, with everything you do not really do removed.
A logic model is a one-page picture of how your program works: inputs (what you put in), activities (what you do), outputs (what you count) and outcomes (what changes).
Ask AI: "Make a logic model table for this program: [public description]. Columns: inputs, activities, outputs, short-term outcomes, long-term outcomes. Keep each cell short."
Then fix it so it matches reality. Remove anything you do not do. A logic model is a plan you can defend, not a wish list.
Step by step:
- Describe the program in three public sentences.
- Ask AI for a logic model table with five columns.
- Remove anything you do not really do.
- Check that each outcome links to an activity.
Words to know:
- Logic model: a one-page table showing inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes.
- Input: what you put into a program: staff, volunteers, money, space.
Try it now: Build a logic model table for your program with AI, then edit it until every cell is true.
You can now build a simple, honest logic model for a program.

check.q: In a logic model, what are activities?
check.why: Activities are what you do; inputs go in, outputs are counted, outcomes are what changes.

check.q: AI's logic model lists a long-term outcome you have no way to reach. What do you do?
options: Keep it; funders like big goals
Remove it so the model matches reality
check.why: A logic model is a plan you can defend, not a wish list.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Choosing outcome measures
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose two outcome measures you can actually collect.
This lesson builds toward: Given an outcome, you will choose two simple measures your team can collect, asked before and after, that are honest and realistic for your staff and volunteer time.
A measure is how you will know an outcome happened. For "families worry less about food", a measure could be: percent of families who say they worried less about running out of food, asked at sign-up and after three months.
Good measures are simple, can be collected by your team, and are honest. Comparing before and after is stronger than asking only once.
Ask AI: "Suggest three simple ways a small nonprofit could measure this outcome: [outcome]. We have [staff and volunteer time]." Pick two you can really do.
Step by step:
- Pick two outcomes from your logic model.
- Ask AI for simple ways to measure each.
- Choose ones your team can collect.
- Plan to measure before and after when you can.
Words to know:
- Measure: how you will know an outcome happened, often a number or percent.
- Before and after: asking the same question at the start and later, to see change.
Try it now: Choose two outcome measures for your program, with AI's suggestions, and write when you will collect each.
You can now choose outcome measures your team can collect.

check.q: Why is asking at sign-up and again later stronger than asking once?
check.why: Comparing before and after shows change.

check.q: AI suggests three measures, but one needs hours of staff time you do not have. What do you do?
options: Pick the two you can really collect
check.why: Good measures can be collected by your team; pick two you can really do.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing a short, fair participant survey
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft a short survey that measures your outcomes.
This lesson builds toward: Given your outcome measures, you will write a short, anonymous participant survey of 5 to 8 questions with AI, with no leading questions and a note that it is voluntary.
A survey asks participants what changed for them. Keep it short, about 5 to 8 questions, in plain words and the languages they use.
Ask AI: "Write a 6-question anonymous survey for adults in our food program to measure [outcome]. Use plain language at a 6th-grade level, mostly multiple choice, one open question. Avoid leading questions."
Remove any question that asks for names, health details or immigration status unless you truly need it and have a safe way to keep it. Tell people the survey is voluntary and will not affect their services. Free tools like Google Forms or Microsoft Forms can collect answers.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for a short anonymous survey that measures your outcome.
- Rewrite any leading question.
- Remove questions about names or sensitive details you do not need.
- Add a note that the survey is voluntary.
- Build it in a free form tool.
Words to know:
- Survey: a set of questions to learn what people think or experienced.
- Anonymous: no names or details that could show who answered.
- Leading question: a question that pushes people toward an answer, like "How much did our great program help you?"
Try it now: Draft a 6-question anonymous survey for your program with AI. Find and rewrite any leading question, and add a voluntary note.
You can now write a short, fair, anonymous participant survey with AI's help.

check.q: What kind of questions should most of the survey use?
options: Mostly multiple choice, with one open question
Only yes or no about the staff
check.why: The prompt asks for mostly multiple choice and one open question.

check.q: AI's survey asks every participant for their health conditions. What do you do?
options: Keep it to get more data
Remove it unless you truly need it and can keep it safely
check.why: Remove questions on health or immigration unless truly needed and safely kept.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Summarizing results without exposing anyone
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Summarize anonymous survey results with AI and check the numbers yourself.
This lesson builds toward: Given anonymous survey counts, you will summarize the results with AI and check every percent yourself, with no detail that could identify a person.
Before using AI on results, make sure the data has no names, contact details or anything else that could identify a person. If a small group could be recognized (for example the only three Spanish-speaking seniors), combine or leave out those details.
Your form tool or spreadsheet can count answers for you. Then you can paste the counts, not raw personal answers, into AI: "Here are survey counts: [counts]. Summarize the main findings in 4 bullet points and suggest one chart."
Check every percent yourself in the spreadsheet. AI often makes math mistakes. For open answers, read them yourself first and remove anything identifying before asking AI to group them into themes.
Step by step:
- Remove names and identifying details.
- Count answers in your form tool or spreadsheet.
- Paste counts, not raw personal answers, into AI.
- Ask for a short summary and a chart idea.
- Check every percent yourself.
Words to know:
- Data: information you collected, like survey answers.
- Theme: an idea that comes up again and again in open answers.
- Percent: a part out of 100, like 60 of 100 people is 60 percent.
Try it now: Use practice counts (for example 30 of 40 people said they worry less about food). Ask AI for a 4-bullet summary, then check each percent with a calculator.
You can now summarize anonymous results with AI and check the numbers.

check.q: What do you do with open answers before asking AI to find themes?
options: Read them yourself and remove anything identifying
Paste them all in as they are
check.why: Read open answers first and remove anything identifying.

check.q: Only two participants are men over 70, so they could be recognized. What do you do?
options: Combine or leave out those details
Ask AI to guess who they are
check.why: If a small group could be recognized, combine or leave out those details.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing a one-page impact report
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your logic model and results into an honest one-page impact report.
This lesson builds toward: Given your logic model and checked results, you will write a one-page impact report with the need, what you did, what changed, a story and a lesson learned, with no numbers or claims that are not in your data.
An impact report tells your board, funders and community what your program did and what changed. One page is enough: the need, what you did (outputs), what changed (outcomes with numbers), one story, and what you learned.
Ask AI: "Using only this information, write a one-page impact report with these headings: The need, What we did, What changed, A story, What we learned. [your logic model, measures, checked results, story shared with permission]."
Include an honest lesson learned. Funders trust organizations that say what did not work and how they will improve. Never let AI add numbers or claims that are not in your data.
Step by step:
- Gather your logic model, measures, checked results and a permitted story.
- Ask AI for a one-page report with five headings, using only your information.
- Check every number against your spreadsheet.
- Add an honest lesson learned.
- Have a colleague read it.
Words to know:
- Impact report: a short report on what a program did and what changed.
- Lesson learned: something you discovered that will help you do better next time.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page impact report with a logic model, two measures, your survey, a summary of anonymous results, a story shared with permission and one honest lesson learned.
You can now plan, measure and report a program's impact with AI's help.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Logic model A column is missing, or it lists things the program does not do. Inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes, all true to the program. Each outcome links clearly to an activity. Outcome measures Measures are outputs, or cannot be collected. Two simple, honest outcome measures the team can collect. Both are asked before and after to show change. Fair survey Leading questions, or it asks for names or sensitive details without need. 5 to 8 plain questions, anonymous and voluntary. Offered in the languages participants use. Anonymous, checked results Results could identify someone, or a percent is wrong. Summary from counts with no identifying details, every percent checked. Open answers are grouped into themes after removing identifying details. Honest one-page report A number or claim is not in the data, or the story has no permission. One page with need, outputs, outcomes, a permitted story and a lesson learned. A colleague read it and the lesson learned says how the program will improve. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which heading belongs in the lesson's one-page impact report?
check.why: The headings are the need, what we did, what changed, a story and what we learned.

check.q: AI's report adds "90% of families found jobs," which is not in your data. What do you do?
options: Remove it, because AI must not add claims that are not in your data
check.why: Never let AI add numbers or claims that are not in your data.
